title: Impact of Sensor Axis Combinations on Machine Learning Accuracy for Human Activity Recognition Using Accelerometer Data in Clinical Settings
content: For diseases such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or arrhythmia, identifying the patient’s activity during symptom onset is crucial for severity assessment and diagnosis. Acceleration data from accelerometers can facilitate this process, but, in clinical settings, minimal data requirements are desirable. The study aimed to determine minimal number of axes needed from a 9-axis accelerometer worn on the non-dominant wrist or chest to maintain high accuracy in recognizing activities related to COPD or arrhythmia. Thirty healthy participants wore 9-axis accelerometers at five positions on their bodies and performed nine activities. We conducted machine learning-based activity recognition using 9-axis, 6-axis, and 3-axis data from the non-dominant wrist or chest. For the non-dominant wrist, 3-axis acceleration data recognized activities such as lying in the supine position, standing, taking a meal, and running, with accuracy comparable to 9-axis data. For the chest, 6-axis combining acceleration and magnetometer recognized activities such as lying in the supine position, standing, sitting, using the restroom, and ascending or descending stairs, with accuracy comparable to 9-axis data. These findings suggest that reducing the axes to 3-axis acceleration for the nondominant wrist and 6-axis combining acceleration and magnetometer for the chest, maintain high activity recognition accuracy.
